newsitem.title: VATICAN: Pope calls for reconciliation between Christians.
newsitem.headline: Pope calls for reconciliation between Christians.

text.p: Pope John Paul, speaking on the eve of an ecumenical conference, appealed for reconciliation between Christians on Sunday and for "open problems" and "unexpected upsets" to be overcome.

A proposed meeting in Austria between the Pontiff and Patriarch Alexiy II, head of the Russian Orthodox Church, before the Second European Ecumenical Conference on Monday in Austria, was called off earlier this month.
It would have been the first meeting of its kind since the Great Schism split Christendom in 1054.
The Pope did not mention the failed meeting in his regular Angelus address and subsequent remarks on Sunday, speaking instead of the importance of reconciliation.
"Reflecting on reconciliation and praying for this is more opportune than ever in a world that still knows so many forms of division," the Pope told Pilgrims in St Peters' Square.
"Reconciliation must involve everyone: Single people, families, nations. All the people of Europe need this, from the Atlantic to the Urals, from East to West," he said.

"In this context, the call for reconciliation among Christians is made with a particular urgency...there are still open problems and sometimes unexpected upsets arise, new worries emerge and unintentional fears come forth."
The Great Schism divided Christendom into Greek and Latin churches after a host of theological disputes.
The Pope has made the quest for greater unity among Christians of different denominations the ambition of his pontificate in the buildup to the start of the new millenium.
On Sunday he said that closer ties on the eve of the third millenium would be "a source of great joy".
More than 10,000 participants from churches across Europe were expected at the ecumenical conference in the southern Austrian town of Graz.
They included the Archbishop of Canterbury, George Carey, who heads the 70-million-strong Anglican Church, and Karekin I, spiritual leader of the world's six million Armenian Christians.

The proposed meeting between the 77-year-old Pope and Alexiy was called off by the Russian Orthodox Church, which said the churches had failed to agree on important issues which needed to be settled before their heads could meet.
